stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the ER with vomiting blood after a night of heavy alcohol drinking. He reports several episodes of retching and nausea prior to the vomiting. He has mild epigastric discomfort but no history of liver disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Retching/vomiting after binge drinking → haematemesis, no liver disease = Mallory–Weiss tear (mucosal tear at the GEJ; 90% stop spontaneously).

why.D: Boerhaave = full-thickness rupture → severe chest pain, sepsis, surgical emphysema — not just haematemesis.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive difficulty swallowing. Initially, he had trouble with solids, but now he has difficulty with both solids and liquids. He reports unintentional weight loss over the past few months. He has a history of long-term smoking and alcohol use. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Progressive dysphagia that starts with solids and then involves liquids = mechanical obstruction that is getting tighter. With weight loss, age 60, smoking and alcohol → oesophageal cancer (SCC).

why.A: Achalasia causes dysphagia to solids AND liquids from the start, usually in younger patients.
why.C: GERD causes heartburn; dysphagia means a complication.
why.D: A peptic stricture follows long reflux and doesn't cause marked weight loss; smoking/alcohol point to cancer.

stem: During a Nissen fundoplication, the fundus of the stomach must be mobilized to create a tension-free 360° wrap around the lower esophagus. Which branch of the splenic artery is typically ligated to allow this mobilization?
expl: The short gastric arteries (from the splenic artery) tether the fundus to the spleen — dividing them frees the fundus for a floppy, tension-free 360° wrap.

why.B: The left gastroepiploic runs along the greater curve lower down; it isn't the vessel divided for fundal mobilisation.
why.D: Hilar branches supply the spleen; dividing them would devascularise it.

stem: A 65-year-old male presents with dysphagia to solids, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, and occasional chest discomfort. What is the most appropriate study to confirm the diagnosis?
expl: Elderly patient with dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food and halitosis = Zenker's diverticulum → barium swallow is the diagnostic test (manometry and endoscopy aren't needed).

why.B: Endoscopy can perforate the pouch and isn't needed for the diagnosis.
why.C: Manometry is for achalasia (hard to position at the UES).
why.D: CT isn't the test for a pharyngeal pouch.

stem: A stable patient has pneumomediastinum, and endoscopy shows a contained oesophageal leak (written in the source as "contained oesophageal bleeding"). What is the best management?
expl: A contained oesophageal leak in a stable patient is managed conservatively: NPO, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, PPI, nutrition and close observation; operate if it is uncontained or the patient becomes septic/unstable.
ansText: NPO and IV antibiotics — a contained, stable perforation is managed conservatively (NPO, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, PPI, nutrition, close observation). Operate if uncontained, septic or unstable.

stem: 60 year old male and suspected to have esophageal cancer what's the best way you to reach the diagnosis?
expl: Tissue diagnosis is required — upper endoscopy with biopsy is the definitive test. CT, PET and EUS come afterwards for staging.

why.B: CT stages — it doesn't give histology.
why.D: Manometry is for achalasia/motility.

stem: A 52 years old man presented to the ER department with acute hematemesis. Bleeding esophageal varices were found during upper GI endoscopy. Which one of the following is the most likely to be effective treatment for this Patient?
expl: Acute variceal bleeding is controlled endoscopically — sclerotherapy (keyed) or, preferably today, band ligation — together with vasoactive drugs (octreotide) and antibiotics.

why.A: Balloon tamponade is a temporary bridge when endoscopy fails.
why.D: Adrenaline injection is for ulcer bleeding.

stem: 45 year old male post-sleeve gastrectomy. On follow up the patient is complaining of extreme reflux. The reflux is severely impacting the patient’s life. His current BMI is 40. What would you recommend?

opts.t: Double the dose of his PPI treatment

expl: Severe GERD after sleeve gastrectomy with persisting obesity (BMI 40) → convert to Roux-en-Y gastric bypass — it cures the reflux and adds weight loss.

why.A: Oesophagectomy is for cancer — far too radical.
why.B: Doubling the PPI may help acid but not volume/bile reflux; the problem is anatomical.
why.C: A balloon worsens reflux and does nothing for GERD.
why.D: Correct.

stem: After oesophagectomy, the surgical drain puts out ~700 mL of serous fluid, which increases and turns white after oral intake. What is the likely cause?
srcNote: Incomplete recall: option A is "??" and options C and D are blank in the source.
expl: After oesophagectomy, drainage that turns milky white once oral (fat) intake starts = chyle leak from thoracic duct injury (chylothorax). Confirmed by the course organiser.
ansText: Thoracic duct injury → chylothorax. Milky fluid appears once fat is eaten (chylomicrons; triglycerides > 110 mg/dL). Treat: NPO/TPN or medium-chain-triglyceride diet ± octreotide; re-operate to ligate the duct if output stays high.

stem: Which of the following is true about dysphagia of achalasia?
srcNote: (Esophageal disorders) Only three answer choices are provided in the source.
expl: Achalasia is a motility disorder — the LES doesn't relax — so solids AND liquids stick from the start (> 90%). Mechanical obstruction affects solids first.

why.C: Liquids alone is not the pattern (pharyngeal/neurological dysphagia).

stem: A surgeon said “Barrett's esophagus” in the OR. Which of the following is associated with this pathology?
srcNote: (Esophageal tumor & esophageal disorders) Incomplete choice set: options C and D appear only as dots in the source.
expl: Barrett's oesophagus is defined by intestinal metaplasia (columnar epithelium with goblet cells) replacing the squamous lining. It also predisposes to adenocarcinoma, but intestinal metaplasia is what the term means.

why.B: An association (premalignant), not the pathology itself; the keyed answer is A.

stem: Type of esophageal diverticula in zenker’s?
expl: Zenker's is a false (pulsion) diverticulum — mucosa and submucosa herniate through Killian's triangle above a hypertonic cricopharyngeus.

why.B: True diverticula contain all layers (traction, mid-oesophageal).
why.C: Traction diverticula are the mid-oesophageal true ones.
why.D: Zenker's is pharyngo-oesophageal (upper).

stem: A patient presented with esophageal variceal bleeding, in examination he has splenomegaly with normal portal vein and liver. What could be the cause?
expl: Splenomegaly with varices but a normal liver and portal vein = left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension — splenic vein thrombosis (often from pancreatitis/pancreatic tumour) → gastric/oesophageal varices. Treated by splenectomy.

why.B: Schistosomiasis causes presinusoidal portal hypertension with periportal fibrosis — the liver isn't normal.
why.C: Budd–Chiari is hepatic vein outflow obstruction — the liver is abnormal (hepatomegaly, ascites).
why.D: Portal hypertensive gastropathy is a consequence, not a cause.

stem: A 55 years old man complained of GERD symptoms, underwent an upper endoscopy that showed severe esophagitis. Biopsy was taken and showed Barrette’s esophagus with severe metaplasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
srcNote: (Esophageal tumor & esophageal disorders) Conflicting source variant: the two-choice recall below gives a different management answer for the same source-described severe metaplasia. Other source key (Final Year not stated Q40 (p. 266)): a. PPI + every six month endoscopy b. PPI + H2 blockers a (Esophageal tumor & esophageal disorders)
expl: Keyed answer: Barrett's with severe oesophagitis means reflux is uncontrolled — anti-reflux surgery (fundoplication) controls the reflux, plus surveillance endoscopy. Metaplasia without dysplasia is never resected. A variant of this recall keyed "PPI + endoscopy every 6 months". The doctor teaches: treat the GERD (PPI or anti-reflux surgery) + surveillance EGD/biopsy every 3–4 years.

why.A: Endoscopy every 3 months is far too frequent for non-dysplastic Barrett's.
why.C: Antibiotics have no role (this isn't H. pylori disease).
why.D: Oesophagectomy is for cancer (or some high-grade dysplasia), not metaplasia.

stem: Patient with variceal bleeding after the initial maintenance of airway, breathing, and circulation. Which intravenous medication has been shown to reduce the mortality incidence in this case?
expl: In variceal bleeding (cirrhosis), prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone) reduce infection, rebleeding and mortality.

why.A: Octreotide controls bleeding but its mortality benefit is less established.
why.D: Correct.

stem: GERD and Achalasia responsible for which cancers respectively?
expl: GERD → Barrett's metaplasia → adenocarcinoma (distal oesophagus). Achalasia → stasis and chronic irritation → squamous cell carcinoma. "Respectively" = adenocarcinoma, then SCC.

why.D: Only half the answer.

stem: Patient with diverticulum in the esophagus. What is the right answer about True diverticulum?

opts.t: Involves all layers of the esophagus
True diverticula are caused by esophageal dysmotility disorders
False diverticula are caused by underlying bronchial pathology
True diverticula are caused by pulsion

expl: A true diverticulum contains all layers of the oesophageal wall (mucosa, submucosa and muscularis); true = traction (mid-oesophagus, from inflamed nodes).

why.D: Pulsion causes false diverticula.

stem: What is type 4 hiatus hernia?

opts.t: Presence of a structure other than stomach such as omentum, colon or small intestine.
Presence of stomach and part of the esophagus

expl: Type IV hiatus hernia = another organ besides the stomach (omentum, colon, small bowel, spleen) herniates through the hiatus.

why.D: Stomach + GEJ above the diaphragm = type III (mixed).

stem: A young male patient, who is known to have liver cirrhosis and esophageal varices presented with complaint of vomiting blood. After initial fluid resuscitation, which one of the following is your treatment of choice for this patient?
expl: Acute variceal bleeding after resuscitation → vasoactive drug (octreotide/terlipressin) to lower portal pressure + antibiotics, then endoscopic band ligation.

why.A: Propranolol is for prevention (primary/secondary), not the acute bleed (it lowers BP in a shocked patient).
why.D: A PPI is not the treatment of variceal bleeding.

stem: A 30-year-old patient presented with intermittent dysphagia for last 5 years. Upper Gl endoscopy showed dilated esophagus with tight lower esophageal sphincter. The was patient submitted for esophageal manometry study. Which one of the following is the expected finding in this procedure?
expl: Achalasia on manometry: hypertensive LES, incomplete or absent LES relaxation, and absent peristalsis in the distal body.

why.C: Contractions are weak/absent or spastic, never normal — "increased contractility" isn't the finding (type III has spasm but no peristalsis).
why.D: Relaxation is incomplete.

stem: Pt newly diagnosed with liver cirrhosis on endoscopy there were visible esophageal varices. How would you prevent the first bleed of the varices?
expl: Primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding = a non-selective β-blocker (propranolol/nadolol/carvedilol) or band ligation for large varices.

why.D: Cimetidine doesn't prevent variceal bleeding.

stem: Patient suspected to have achalasia, which test is used to confirm the diagnosis?
expl: Manometry is the gold standard for achalasia (a muscle-function disease). Barium shows the bird's beak; endoscopy rules out pseudo-achalasia (cancer).

why.C: Needed to exclude malignancy, but normal in 50% of achalasia.
why.D: pH study is for GERD.

stem: A patient has a Barret’s esophagus and is asking you about what type of cancer is caused by his condition?
srcNote: (Esophageal tumor & esophageal disorders) 437A Incomplete choice set: option D is blank in the source.
expl: Barrett's (intestinal metaplasia of the distal oesophagus) progresses through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma.

why.A: SCC is linked to smoking, alcohol, achalasia and caustics — not Barrett's.

stem: A 75 year old patient diagnosed to have esophageal carcinoma. TNM staging showed that his disease is stage 3, he also has a history of heart failure. Which ONE of the following is the management of choice?
srcNote: (Esophageal tumor & esophageal disorders) Stage and certainty differ in a merged recall; the stage 3 source question is retained above. Other source key (Final 436 A Q17): The source variant states: "stage 2 (wasn’t 3)". A. Palliative therapy. Answer: Not sure A (Esophageal tumor & esophageal disorders)
expl: An elderly patient with heart failure is not fit for oesophagectomy (one of the most morbid operations) or aggressive multimodal therapy → palliation (stent, palliative RT ± chemo). One recall version said stage 2, keyed "not sure A".

why.B: Radiotherapy alone isn't curative here; it is one palliative tool.
why.D: Chemotherapy alone isn't curative; poorly tolerated with heart failure.

stem: A 50-year-old male newly diagnosed with early esophageal cancer. What is his most likely presenting symptoms?
expl: The main symptom of oesophageal cancer is progressive dysphagia (with weight loss). Truly early lesions are often silent, but of these options dysphagia is the presenting symptom.

why.C: Chest pain is less common and later.
why.D: Constipation is unrelated.

stem: An 80-year old male with pharyngoesophageal (Zenker's) diverticulum was referred to your clinic. Which symptoms are most likely to be present in this patent?
expl: Food retained in a Zenker's pouch decomposes → halitosis; also regurgitation of undigested food, gurgling, cough and aspiration.

why.D: Patients regurgitate undigested food rather than true vomiting.

stem: 45 year old patient complaining of chest discomfort and heartburn, smoking and stress aggravate it, physical exam shows overweight patient and the rest is unremarkable, what is the diagnosis?
expl: Heartburn and chest discomfort worsened by smoking/stress in an overweight patient with a normal exam = GERD.

why.B: Achalasia presents with dysphagia to solids and liquids and regurgitation.
why.C: Cancer presents with dysphagia and weight loss.
why.D: A hiatal hernia can cause GERD, but the clinical diagnosis from these symptoms is GERD.

stem: A 50-year old man with a history of chronic alcoholism presents with hematemesis preceded by episodes of violent and repeated vomiting. The patient has significant chest pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Violent repeated vomiting followed by haematemesis and significant chest pain in an alcoholic = Boerhaave's syndrome (full-thickness rupture, usually the left posterolateral distal oesophagus). Mackler's triad: vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema.

why.A: MI doesn't cause haematemesis after vomiting.
why.C: Mallory–Weiss is a mucosal tear — bleeding without severe chest pain/sepsis.
why.D: Varices bleed without preceding retching and chest pain.

stem: A 60 y/o man was admitted with marked weight loss due to carcinoma of the lower esophagus. Which of the following is the appropriate method to improve his nutritional status before surgery?
srcNote: ( Miscellaneous ) Conflicting source keys: the retained preoperative question gives B; the two related nutrition recalls below give C. Their stems do not explicitly say "before surgery". Other source key (Midterm 429 F Q30): C. Gastrostomy feeding (this is for long TERM) C (Nutrition in surgical patients) Patient can use his GI system, but it was answered as TPN. Other source key (Midterm 428 Q6): C. Gastrostomy feeding C, Patient still can use his GI.
expl: Source key: central parenteral nutrition. Reasoning used by the key: an obstructing lower esophageal cancer limits enteral access, and a gastrostomy would damage the stomach needed as the esophageal conduit. (Another version of this question keyed gastrostomy because the gut is usable.)

why.A: Peripheral PN cannot deliver enough calories for marked weight loss.
why.C: Keyed in the 429 version; the stomach is usually preserved for reconstruction.
why.D: A tube may not pass an obstructing tumor.

stem: A 50 year old man with history of chronic alcoholism presents with hematemesis after episodes of violent and repeated vomiting, the patient has significant chest pain. On examination the patient is in shock * Which of the following findings is likely associated with his condition?
expl: Boerhaave's rupture lets air into the mediastinum → subcutaneous (surgical) emphysema in the neck/chest (Mackler's triad); shock comes from mediastinitis/sepsis.

why.D: Jaundice = liver disease (not this picture).

stem: A 32- year-old alcoholic male patient is brought to the emergency department with a history of vomiting large amount of bright red blood. Physical examination revealed splenomegaly and ascites. Which of the following is the most likely source of bleeding?
srcNote: (liver and splenic diseases and pancreatic masses)
expl: An alcoholic with massive bright red haematemesis, splenomegaly and ascites has portal hypertension → oesophageal varices.

why.A: Duodenal ulcer doesn't explain splenomegaly and ascites.
why.B: Gastric ulcer doesn't explain splenomegaly and ascites.
why.D: Gastric cancer doesn't explain splenomegaly and ascites.

stem: all are a predisposition for esophageal cancer except:
srcNote: Incomplete duplicate: Final 427 F Q27 lists four choices (A-D), omits Achalasia, and still states "Answer: E". The complete five-choice Midterm version is retained above.
expl: Achalasia, Plummer-Vinson, Barrett's and corrosive injury all predispose to esophageal cancer; a simple esophageal cyst does not.

why.D: Predisposes (SCC).

stem: All predispose to malignancy except:
expl: Achalasia, Plummer–Vinson syndrome and Barrett's are premalignant oesophageal conditions; an oesophageal cyst (duplication/inclusion cyst) is benign with no malignant potential.

why.D: Barrett's → adenocarcinoma.

stem: Barret’s esophagus except
srcNote: , incomplete Q Incomplete source recall: only two answer choices are provided.
expl: Barrett's is premalignant but is managed with surveillance ± endoscopic therapy; it is not resected at the metaplasia stage.

stem: all are esophageal benign tumor except
expl: Leiomyoma (most common), fibrovascular polyp and papilloma are benign; leiomyosarcoma is malignant.

why.D: Benign.

stem: Palliative treatment for esophageal cancer all except

opts.t: surgery Stent is long term effective palliative
radiotherapy high beam is very effective
Cisplatin can be used surgical palliative resection
can be used for selective patients

srcNote: , don’t know why “incomplete Q” Incomplete source recall: the option wording is fragmented and the source explicitly questions its answer key. No missing text has been supplied.
expl: The question is incomplete; the source key is B. Palliation of esophageal cancer uses stents, brachytherapy/radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

why.A: Option text garbled in the source.
why.C: Option text garbled in the source.
why.D: Option text garbled in the source.

stem: All except bleeding varices: “incomplete Q”
srcNote: Incomplete source recall: the stem is unclear, and "Urgent" and "endoscopy" appear as separate numbered choices in the original. The source wording and five choices are preserved.
expl: The recall is incomplete, but the key is clear: bleeding varices are managed with ABC, urgent endoscopy, drugs and balloon tamponade/TIPS — immediate laparotomy is not part of it (surgical shunts are a late last resort).

why.A: Bilharziasis is a cause of varices (in the region).
why.C: Urgent endoscopy is part of management.
why.D: Endoscopy is part of management.

stem: Esophageal varices can be treated by all except
expl: Varices are treated by endoscopic sclerotherapy or band ligation, balloon tamponade, drugs and TIPS. "Electrotherapy" is not a variceal treatment (keyed). Cautery/thermal coagulation is used for ulcers and isn't ideal for varices either, but the key is electrotherapy.

why.A: Not standard for varices, but not the keyed answer.
why.D: Balloon tamponade controls the bleeding temporarily.

stem: A 52 years old man presented to ER with acute hematemesis. Bleeding esophageal varices were found during upper GI endoscopy. The patient did not response to endoscopic treatment Bp 80/40 HR 160, which of the following is the most likely to be effective treatment for this patient?
srcNote: not known. Minnesota tube is used as a way to control bleeding not to treat. Unanswered source question: the source states that the answer is not known. Only three choices are provided.
expl: The source had no key. When endoscopic therapy fails in an unstable patient, balloon tamponade (Minnesota/Sengstaken–Blakemore tube) controls the bleeding as a bridge to definitive therapy (TIPS). Octreotide should already be running; oesophagectomy has no role.

why.B: Octreotide is given from the start — escalating it doesn't stop a torrential bleed.
why.C: Correct (added) — tamponade as a bridge to TIPS.
